subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of a curve whose gradient is dy/dx = y/x − cos²(y/x), which passes through the point (1, π/4).

mark_split.label: Apply the given point and finish

insider_note: The curve is given by its gradient, not by an equation in x and y, so the very first move is to treat dy/dx = y/x − cos²(y/x) as the differential equation to solve, and the point (1, π/4) is used only at the very last step to fix the constant.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The right side already depends only on the ratio y/x, so the equation is homogeneous by inspection.
steps.memory_tip: y/x − cos²(y/x) is written entirely in terms of v = y/x — no separate substitution work needed to see that.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx = y/x − cos²(y/x) … (1)
Put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx
steps.why: A gradient given purely in terms of y/x is already homogeneous, so substituting y = vx and dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx immediately turns the equation into one for v alone.
common_mistakes: Trying to expand cos²(y/x) instead of directly replacing y/x by v.
Forgetting to replace dy/dx by v + x·dv/dx before substituting on the right.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. The two copies of v cancel completely, leaving a clean equation in cos²v alone.
steps.memory_tip: v on both sides of the equation always cancels first, before anything else — look for that cancellation.
steps.why: The two v terms cancel exactly, leaving x·dv/dx = −cos²v; dividing by −cos²v and taking the reciprocal gives sec²v dv on the left, separated from dx/x on the right.
common_mistakes: Missing the cancellation of the two v terms and carrying an extra v through the rest of the working.
Writing 1/cos²v as cos²v instead of sec²v.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. ∫sec²v dv = tan v is a standard integral; the right side needs a sign flip.
steps.memory_tip: sec²v integrates to tan v directly — no substitution needed on the left.
steps.why: sec²v is the derivative of tan v, so the left side integrates directly; the minus sign carried from the separation step lands on the log|x| term on the right.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign in front of log|x|.
Writing the integral of sec²v as sec v tan v instead of tan v.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Move the log term to the left before substituting v = y/x.
steps.memory_tip: tan v + log|x| = c is the general family — the given point fixes c next.
lines: Put v = y/x: tan(y/x) + log|x| = c
steps.why: Rearranging tan v = −log|x| + c into tan v + log|x| = c gives the general family of curves in the ratio v, and substituting v = y/x writes it back in terms of the original x and y.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to move the −log|x| across to the left, leaving the sign wrong in the general family.
Substituting v = y/x into the earlier, uncombined line instead of the rearranged one.

steps.label: Apply the given point and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Substitute x = 1, y = π/4 to find c, then write the final particular solution.
steps.memory_tip: log|1| = 0 and tan(π/4) = 1 — both simplify away instantly at this point.
lines: If the curve passes through (x, y) = (1, π/4), then
steps.why: Substituting the given point into the general family fixes the arbitrary constant, and putting that value of c back into (2) gives the one curve through (1, π/4), which is what the question actually asks for.
common_mistakes: Substituting the point into the original differential equation instead of into the integrated family (2).
Evaluating tan(π/4) as an approximate decimal instead of the exact value 1.
